explanation: Composite alarms combine related alarms to reduce noise—a service is truly degraded only when multiple indicators alarm simultaneously. Severity-based routing ensures critical issues reach on-call teams immediately while informational alerts go to lower-priority channels. Increasing thresholds (B) may cause missed genuine issues and provides a blanket approach. Anomaly detection (C) is useful but may still generate noise from expected anomalies. Dashboard monitoring (D) is reactive and doesn't work outside business hours.

stem: A company is modernizing a legacy batch processing system that generates weekly business reports. The system reads from multiple MySQL databases, joins data across databases, applies complex aggregations, and produces CSV and PDF output. The current process takes 8 hours on a dedicated server. The company wants to reduce processing time to under 2 hours using AWS services. Which architecture achieves this performance improvement?

options.text: Use AWS Glue ETL with multiple DPUs for parallel data extraction from MySQL databases, Spark-based joins and aggregations in Glue, and generate output files directly from the Glue job to S3.
Use DMS to replicate all MySQL databases to a single Redshift cluster, run aggregation queries in Redshift using its MPP engine, and export results to S3 for CSV and PDF generation.
Use Lambda functions to query each MySQL database in parallel, aggregate results in DynamoDB, run final aggregation queries against DynamoDB, and generate CSV and PDF output with Lambda.
Migrate the batch processing scripts to an EC2 instance with more CPU and memory than the on-premises server, install MySQL clients for direct database queries, and run the existing scripts.

explanation: Glue ETL with multiple DPUs provides distributed Spark processing that parallelizes data extraction, joins, and aggregations across databases. This can reduce 8-hour sequential processing to under 2 hours through parallelism. Lambda (B) has timeout limitations for complex multi-database joins and aggregations. DMS to Redshift (C) adds ongoing replication overhead for a weekly job. Bigger EC2 (D) helps marginally but doesn't fundamentally change the sequential processing architecture.

stem: A company operates a multi-account environment where development teams frequently need to test with production-like data. The company cannot copy production data to development due to PII regulations. The company needs to provide development teams with realistic test data that has the same statistical properties as production data but contains no actual PII. Which approach provides safe test data generation?

options.text: Use AWS Glue DataBrew PII detection and redaction recipes to identify and mask PII fields in production data exports, replace PII with anonymized values, and provide sanitized copies to development.
Create a DMS migration task that copies production data to development accounts with transformation rules that replace PII columns with randomly generated data matching the column data types.
Use Amazon Macie to identify S3 buckets containing PII, restrict development account access to those buckets via bucket policies, and provide development teams with metadata only for testing.
Copy production database snapshots to development accounts, use RDS encryption with development-specific KMS keys, and restrict developer query access to non-PII columns using database views.

explanation: Glue DataBrew can detect PII using built-in and custom identifiers, then apply masking recipes that replace PII with realistic anonymized values while preserving data statistical properties. This creates safe test datasets. DMS transformation rules (B) can modify data but lack sophisticated PII detection and realistic replacement generation. Macie (C) identifies PII locations but doesn't create anonymized test data. Copying snapshots with restricted views (D) still contains actual PII in the database, violating the regulation.

stem: A company is building an edge computing platform for autonomous vehicle testing. Vehicles collect 4 TB of sensor data per day and need to run ML inference models locally for real-time object detection. Vehicles are intermittently connected to the cloud. When connected, they must upload sensor data and download updated ML models. Which architecture supports both edge inference and cloud synchronization?

options.text: Deploy SageMaker Neo-compiled models on custom hardware in vehicles, use AWS DataSync to upload sensor data to S3 when connected, and push new models via Systems Manager Run Command.
Use AWS IoT Greengrass on in-vehicle compute for local ML inference, configure Greengrass stream manager for data upload to S3 when connected, and deploy updated models via Greengrass OTA.
Use AWS Snowball Edge devices in each vehicle for local compute and storage, run SageMaker edge models on Snowball, and ship Snowball devices to AWS data centers weekly for data sync.
Use Lambda@Edge deployed to CloudFront edge locations near testing areas, route vehicle requests to the nearest edge location for inference, and upload data directly to S3 via Transfer Acceleration.

explanation: IoT Greengrass provides local ML inference on edge devices with intermittent connectivity. Stream manager handles store-and-forward data upload when connected. OTA deployment updates ML models remotely. This is the standard edge computing pattern for vehicles. SageMaker Neo (B) compiles models but SSM Run Command requires network connectivity for model deployment. Snowball Edge (C) requires physical device shipping for data sync, which is impractical for daily vehicle data. Lambda@Edge (D) runs at CloudFront locations, not in vehicles, and requires constant connectivity.

stem: A company with 200 AWS accounts must restrict all S3 buckets to private access only across the entire Organization. The policy must prevent any S3 bucket from being made public, even by account administrators. Existing public buckets must be identified and remediated. Which approach provides both preventive and detective controls?

options.text: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the Organization level using the S3 console for each account individually, deploy Config rules to detect public buckets, and send alerts to the security team.

Deploy AWS Config managed rules for s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited and s3-bucket-public-write-prohibited across all accounts with auto-remediation Lambda to enable Block Public Access on violating buckets.
Create IAM policies in each account that deny s3:PutBucketAcl and s3:PutBucketPolicy with public access grants, distribute via StackSets, and use Macie to scan for publicly accessible content.
Use an SCP that denies s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock with specific conditions, enable S3 Block Public Access at the Organization level via Organizations API, and deploy Config rules for detection.

explanation: S3 Block Public Access at the Organization level prevents any bucket from being made public across all accounts. The SCP prevents anyone from disabling this setting. Config rules detect any existing public buckets for remediation. Per-account Block Public Access (A) can be disabled by account admins without an SCP. Config rules alone (C) are reactive, not preventive. IAM policies per account (D) can be modified by administrators and don't cover all public access paths.

stem: A healthcare company needs to build a FHIR-compliant API for exchanging patient health records with hospitals and clinics. The API must support the HL7 FHIR R4 standard, handle 10,000 requests per second, and store patient data in a HIPAA-compliant manner. The company wants to minimize the development effort for FHIR compliance. Which architecture reduces the FHIR implementation effort?

options.text: Deploy the HAPI FHIR server on ECS Fargate with Aurora PostgreSQL for data storage, configure ALB for traffic management, enable ACM certificates for HTTPS, and implement custom FHIR APIs.
Use Amazon API Gateway with AppSync resolvers that map FHIR API calls to DynamoDB queries, implement FHIR validation using Lambda middleware, and use Cognito for OAuth2 client authentication.
Use AWS HealthLake to create a FHIR-compliant data store, configure HealthLake APIs for FHIR resource CRUD operations, use API Gateway for client authentication, and enable encryption at rest.
Build a custom FHIR API on API Gateway with Lambda, implement FHIR R4 resource types in Lambda functions, store data in DynamoDB with a schema matching FHIR resources, and add Cognito auth.

explanation: HealthLake provides a purpose-built FHIR R4-compliant data store with built-in FHIR APIs, eliminating the need to implement FHIR resource handling. It's HIPAA-eligible and supports natural language processing on health data. API Gateway adds authentication. Custom FHIR API (B) requires implementing the entire FHIR specification. HAPI FHIR on ECS (C) requires deploying and managing the FHIR server infrastructure. AppSync with DynamoDB (D) requires building FHIR compliance from scratch.

stem: A company runs a web application on EC2 instances behind an ALB. The application stores user-uploaded files on EBS volumes attached to each instance. When an instance terminates during scale-in events, files stored on that instance's EBS volume are lost. The company needs shared, persistent storage accessible by all instances without changing the application's file system interface. Which storage migration preserves the file system interface?

options.text: Configure EBS Multi-Attach on io2 volumes shared between instances, update the application to use a cluster-aware file system like GFS2, and mount the shared volume on all running instances.
Deploy Amazon FSx for Lustre as a high-performance shared file system, mount it on all instances, and configure S3 data repository integration for durable storage of uploaded files.
Migrate files to S3 and modify the application to use the AWS SDK for file operations, replacing local file system calls with S3 PutObject and GetObject API calls throughout the codebase.
Migrate uploaded files to Amazon EFS mounted on all instances using NFS, update the application's upload directory path to the EFS mount point, and use EFS lifecycle management for cost optimization.

explanation: EFS provides a shared NFS file system that mounts like a local directory, preserving the application's file system interface. All instances access the same files. Lifecycle management moves infrequently accessed files to lower-cost storage. S3 (B) requires changing the application from file system to API calls. EBS Multi-Attach (C) requires a cluster-aware file system, adding complexity. FSx for Lustre (D) is designed for HPC workloads and is over-provisioned for user file uploads.

stem: A company is migrating a microservices application that uses Netflix OSS stack (Eureka for service discovery, Zuul for API gateway, Hystrix for circuit breaking, Ribbon for load balancing) to AWS. The company wants to replace the Netflix components with AWS-managed equivalents to reduce operational overhead. Which mapping of AWS services replaces the Netflix OSS stack?

options.text: Replace Eureka with Route 53 DNS, Zuul with CloudFront, Hystrix with SNS dead-letter queues for failure handling, and Ribbon with NLB round-robin load balancing for service instances.
Replace Eureka with Cloud Map, Zuul with API Gateway, Hystrix circuit breaking with App Mesh retry/timeout policies, and Ribbon with ALB target group load balancing across services.
Replace the entire Netflix stack with AWS App Runner which handles service discovery, load balancing, and traffic management automatically, and add Lambda for circuit breaking logic.
Keep all Netflix OSS components running on ECS containers, add CloudWatch for monitoring Netflix components, and gradually migrate to AWS services one component at a time over 18 months.

explanation: Cloud Map provides service discovery (replacing Eureka). API Gateway replaces Zuul for API routing. App Mesh provides circuit breaking, retries, and timeouts (replacing Hystrix). ALB provides client-side load balancing equivalent to Ribbon. All are managed services reducing operational overhead. Route 53/CloudFront/SNS (B) don't map to the Netflix components functionally. Keeping Netflix OSS (C) doesn't reduce operational overhead. App Runner (D) doesn't provide circuit breaking or fine-grained traffic management comparable to the Netflix stack.

stem: A company needs to establish a secure pipeline for developers to build and deploy container images. The pipeline must scan images for vulnerabilities before deployment, ensure only signed images can be deployed to production EKS clusters, and maintain an audit trail of all image deployments. Which architecture implements a secure container image pipeline?

options.text: Use ECR with CodeBuild for image builds, scan with Trivy in the build pipeline, store scan results in S3, and configure EKS pod security policies to restrict which registries pods can pull from.
Use ECR with Amazon Inspector for continuous vulnerability scanning, implement image tag immutability, deploy to EKS using Helm charts with pinned image digests, and audit through CloudTrail.
Use ECR with image scanning on push for vulnerability detection, configure ECR image signing with AWS Signer, enforce signature verification in EKS using admission controllers, and log to CloudTrail.
Use Docker Hub for image storage, scan images with Snyk in the CI pipeline, manually verify image hashes before deployment, and log deployment events in CloudWatch Logs for audit tracking.

explanation: ECR image scanning detects vulnerabilities at push time. AWS Signer provides cryptographic image signing. EKS admission controllers enforce that only signed images can be deployed to production. CloudTrail provides the complete audit trail. Docker Hub (B) is external and manual hash verification doesn't scale. Inspector scanning with tag immutability (C) provides scanning but doesn't enforce cryptographic signature verification before deployment. Trivy scanning (D) is part of the build but doesn't enforce signature-based deployment control.

stem: A company is designing a high-throughput data ingestion pipeline that receives JSON events from 100,000 sources. Each event is 1-10 KB. The pipeline must validate event schemas, enrich events with reference data, transform events into a standard format, and load them into both a real-time analytics engine and a data lake. Total throughput is 1 million events per second. Which architecture handles this throughput?

options.text: Use Kinesis Data Streams for ingestion with 1000 shards, Lambda for schema validation and enrichment reading reference data from DynamoDB, and fan out to OpenSearch and S3 via Firehose.
Use API Gateway to receive events, SQS for buffering, Lambda for validation and transformation, write to Kinesis Data Firehose for S3 delivery, and use Athena for real-time analytics.
Use Amazon MSK for event ingestion, Kafka Streams on ECS for schema validation and enrichment, sink to OpenSearch using Kafka Connect, and use S3 Sink Connector for data lake storage.
Use Amazon EventBridge for event routing with schema registry validation, enrich events using EventBridge input transformers, and route to both OpenSearch and S3 using EventBridge targets.

explanation: Kinesis Data Streams with 1000 shards handles 1M events/sec (1000 records/sec per shard). Lambda validates and enriches using DynamoDB for fast reference lookups. Kinesis enhanced fan-out sends to multiple consumers: OpenSearch for real-time analytics and Firehose for S3 data lake. API Gateway (B) has request rate limits and Athena isn't real-time analytics. MSK (C) works but requires more operational management than Kinesis for this use case. EventBridge (D) has throughput limits well below 1M events/sec.

stem: A company uses Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with multiple read replicas for its application. The application uses a single writer endpoint for all queries including both writes and reads. This causes the writer to be overloaded while read replicas sit idle. The company wants to distribute read traffic to replicas without modifying application code. Which solution redirects read queries to replicas transparently?

options.text: Configure the application to use the Aurora reader endpoint for SELECT queries and the writer endpoint for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE queries by modifying the database connection configuration.
Deploy Amazon RDS Proxy with read/write split configuration, point the application to the RDS Proxy endpoint, and let RDS Proxy automatically route reads to replicas and writes to the writer.
Deploy ProxySQL on EC2 instances between the application and Aurora, configure query rules to route SELECT queries to read replicas and write queries to the primary writer instance.
Create a custom Aurora endpoint with a READER type that includes all read replicas, configure the application's read connection pool to use this endpoint for load distribution.

explanation: RDS Proxy with read/write splitting automatically routes read queries to replicas and write queries to the writer without application code changes. The application connects to a single proxy endpoint. Modifying connection strings (B) requires application code changes. Custom reader endpoint (C) still requires the application to choose which endpoint to use. ProxySQL on EC2 (D) requires managing additional infrastructure.

stem: A company is modernizing its monolithic application by extracting the user authentication module as the first microservice. The monolith currently handles authentication with a local user database and session cookies. The new auth microservice must support the existing cookie-based sessions for the monolith while also providing JWT tokens for new microservices. Which approach enables this dual authentication during the transition?

options.text: Replace all session cookies with JWTs immediately across the monolith and new microservices, update the monolith code to validate JWTs instead of session cookies, and use Cognito for issuance.
Keep the monolith's authentication unchanged, deploy API Gateway with Cognito authorizer for new microservices only, and plan to migrate the monolith to Cognito after all services are extracted.
Build a custom auth service on ECS that maintains the session cookie mechanism for the monolith and also issues JWTs for new services, backed by the same user database migrated to Aurora.
Deploy Amazon Cognito as the auth microservice, use hosted UI for authentication, issue both session cookies for the monolith via Lambda@Edge and JWT tokens for microservices via Cognito.

explanation: A custom auth service maintains backward compatibility with the monolith's session cookies while providing JWTs for new microservices. Using the same user database ensures consistent authentication during the transition. Cognito (A) doesn't natively support custom session cookie issuance for legacy monoliths. Keeping auth unchanged (C) means the auth module is never extracted as a microservice. Immediate JWT replacement (D) requires modifying the monolith code, contradicting the gradual extraction approach.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with 100 accounts organized into OUs for different business divisions. The company needs to implement guardrails that automatically apply when accounts are moved between OUs. For example, when an account moves from the development OU to the production OU, production-specific SCPs and security configurations must be applied automatically. Which mechanism ensures configurations follow OU membership?

options.text: Attach SCPs directly to each OU so they inherit automatically when accounts move, use CloudFormation StackSets with OU-level targeting for configurations, and Control Tower guardrails per OU.
Maintain a mapping table in DynamoDB that tracks which configurations apply to each OU, run a daily reconciliation Lambda that compares actual vs desired state and applies missing configurations.
Create EventBridge rules that detect MoveAccount API calls, trigger Lambda functions that apply the correct SCPs and deploy configurations based on the target OU identification in the event.
Assign tags to accounts based on their OU membership, create tag-based AWS Config rules that evaluate compliance based on the account's current OU tag, and remediate non-compliant accounts.

explanation: SCPs attached to OUs automatically apply to any account in that OU. When accounts move, they inherit the new OU's SCPs immediately. StackSets with OU-level targeting deploy configurations based on OU membership. Control Tower guardrails provide additional enforcement per OU. EventBridge with Lambda (B) adds complexity when native OU inheritance handles SCPs automatically. Daily reconciliation (C) creates a gap between OU change and configuration application. Tag-based approaches (D) require maintaining tags separately from OU membership.

stem: A company needs to build a secure API that accepts file uploads up to 5 GB from external partners. The API must validate file types, scan files for malware, and store clean files in S3. The upload must support resumable uploads for large files over unreliable connections. The company wants to minimize the data flowing through their application layer. Which architecture handles large file uploads efficiently?

options.text: Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint for partner file uploads to S3, configure partner-specific home directories, trigger a Step Functions workflow on upload for validation and malware scanning.
Deploy an EC2-based upload service behind an NLB that accepts large file uploads via HTTP, validate file types and scan for malware during upload, and stream clean files to S3 using multipart upload.
Accept file uploads through API Gateway with a 10 MB payload limit, chunk large files in the client, reassemble chunks in Lambda, validate and scan the complete file, and store in S3.
Generate S3 pre-signed URLs for multipart upload via API Gateway, have partners upload directly to S3, trigger Lambda on upload completion for file type validation and ClamAV malware scanning.

explanation: Pre-signed URLs allow partners to upload directly to S3 via multipart upload, supporting resumable 5 GB uploads without data flowing through the application layer. Lambda triggers on upload completion for validation and scanning. API Gateway payload limit (B) is 10 MB, requiring complex chunking. EC2 upload service (C) requires all data to flow through the application layer. Transfer Family SFTP (D) works but doesn't support resumable HTTP uploads that web clients expect.

stem: A company migrated its application to AWS 6 months ago using a lift-and-shift approach. The application runs on m5.2xlarge EC2 instances. AWS Compute Optimizer shows that instances average 15% CPU utilization with peaks of 40%. Memory utilization averages 25%. The company wants to right-size the instances without risking performance degradation during peak hours. Which approach provides safe right-sizing?

options.text: Migrate all workloads to Lambda functions to eliminate the need for instance sizing entirely, using API Gateway to route requests to Lambda and eliminating always-on infrastructure costs.
Switch to m5.xlarge instances (one size down) as a conservative first step, monitor for 2 weeks using CloudWatch detailed monitoring, and continue right-sizing if metrics remain healthy.
Immediately switch all instances to t3.medium burstable instances based on the low average utilization, relying on CPU credits to handle the occasional 40% utilization peaks during busy periods.
Follow Compute Optimizer recommendations to downsize to m5.large instances, deploy the change in the staging environment first, load test at peak levels, and then apply to production gradually.

explanation: Reducing one instance size conservatively addresses the over-provisioning while maintaining a safety margin for peaks. Two weeks of monitoring validates the change before further optimization. This is the safe iterative right-sizing approach. Jumping to m5.large (A) based on averages may not handle peak loads safely. Burstable t3.medium (B) risks running out of CPU credits during sustained peaks. Lambda migration (D) is a major architecture change, not a right-sizing exercise.

stem: A company is modernizing a legacy application that uses cron jobs for task scheduling. The application has 50 different scheduled tasks running at various intervals from every minute to once a week. Tasks include database maintenance, report generation, data synchronization, and email notifications. The company wants a managed scheduling solution that eliminates the cron server. Which service replaces the cron-based scheduling?

options.text: Use CloudWatch Events rules with cron expressions for scheduling, configure all targets as SQS queues, and deploy a single Lambda function that polls all queues and dispatches appropriate tasks.
Use AWS Systems Manager Maintenance Windows for all scheduled tasks, configure targets as Lambda functions or SSM Run Command on EC2 instances, and set maintenance window schedules.
Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler with rate and cron expressions for each task, configure Lambda functions as targets for short tasks, and use ECS Fargate tasks for longer-running operations.
Deploy a single EC2 instance running cron daemon with all 50 cron jobs migrated, configure Auto Recovery for high availability, and use CloudWatch agent for monitoring cron job execution.

explanation: EventBridge Scheduler provides managed cron and rate-based scheduling with support for various targets including Lambda and ECS Fargate. Lambda handles short tasks while ECS Fargate handles longer-running operations. No server management required. EC2 with cron (B) still requires server management. SSM Maintenance Windows (C) are designed for maintenance tasks, not general application scheduling. CloudWatch Events with SQS (D) adds unnecessary complexity with queue-based indirection.

stem: A company needs to ensure that its AWS environment is protected against both network-level DDoS attacks and application-level attacks. The company runs public-facing applications behind ALBs and CloudFront distributions. The company also needs access to the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) for assistance during attacks. Which TWO services should be implemented together for comprehensive DDoS protection?

options.text: AWS Shield Advanced for enhanced DDoS protection on ALBs and CloudFront distributions with automatic mitigation, cost protection, and 24/7 access to the DDoS Response Team for incidents.
AWS Network Firewall deployed in each VPC for stateful packet inspection of all inbound traffic, configured with intrusion detection rules to identify and block DDoS attack patterns.
AWS WAF with rate-limiting rules and managed rule groups for OWASP Top 10 protection on ALBs and CloudFront distributions, providing application-layer inspection and bot mitigation.
Amazon GuardDuty with threat intelligence feeds for detecting reconnaissance activities that precede DDoS attacks, configured to alert the security team before attacks begin.

explanation: Shield Advanced provides network-layer DDoS protection with automatic mitigation, cost protection during attacks, and DRT access. WAF provides application-layer protection with rate limiting, bot control, and OWASP rules. Together they cover both network and application-layer attacks. Network Firewall (C) is for VPC traffic inspection, not DDoS-specific protection on ALBs/CloudFront. GuardDuty (D) detects threats but doesn't provide DDoS mitigation capabilities.

stem: A company is designing a multi-player game backend that must synchronize game state between players in real-time. The game has rooms with up to 50 players each, requiring sub-50ms state propagation. Players can join and leave rooms dynamically. The backend must handle 100,000 concurrent rooms. Which architecture provides real-time state synchronization at this scale?

options.text: Deploy custom game servers on EC2 instances with ENA in placement groups, use UDP for state propagation, manage room assignments in ElastiCache Redis, and use NLB for player connections.
Use Amazon GameLift for game server hosting and matchmaking, deploy game sessions on Spot Instances for cost optimization, and use GameLift Realtime Servers for lightweight state synchronization.
Use AppSync real-time subscriptions for state updates, DynamoDB for game state with DynamoDB Streams triggering AppSync mutations, and Cognito for player authentication and room management.
Use API Gateway WebSocket APIs with Lambda for connection management, DynamoDB for room state, and IoT Core MQTT topics per room for real-time pub/sub state propagation to players.
Placeholder to maintain 4 options.

explanation: Custom EC2 game servers with UDP provide the lowest latency for real-time state propagation (sub-50ms). ElastiCache Redis handles room management with microsecond operations. NLB supports UDP and massive concurrent connections. Placement groups minimize network latency. API Gateway WebSocket with Lambda (A) adds latency through the Lambda invocation chain. AppSync subscriptions (C) use WebSocket which adds overhead compared to UDP. GameLift (D) is for session-based matchmaking games, not persistent rooms with custom state sync at 100K concurrent rooms.

stem: A company has an S3-based data lake with 1 PB of data. The company uses Athena for ad-hoc queries, but analysts report that query costs are high and query times are slow. Investigation reveals that most tables use CSV format without partitioning, and queries frequently scan the entire dataset. Which optimization strategy provides the greatest improvement in both cost and performance?

options.text: Switch from Athena to Redshift Serverless for all queries, load data from S3 using COPY commands, create distribution keys on commonly joined columns, and use Redshift materialized views.
Add Athena result caching by enabling query result reuse, create named queries for common analysis patterns, and increase Athena per-account DML query concurrency limits for faster execution.
Convert all CSV data to Apache Parquet format with Snappy compression, implement partitioning by the most commonly filtered columns, and update Glue Data Catalog with partition metadata.
Enable S3 Select to push predicate filtering to the storage layer for CSV files, implement Athena workgroups with per-query byte scan limits, and educate analysts on efficient query patterns.

explanation: Converting CSV to Parquet provides columnar storage with compression, reducing both scan size and cost by 90%+. Partitioning enables partition pruning, further reducing scanned data. Together these address both cost and performance at the root cause. Redshift Serverless (B) requires data loading and adds service complexity. S3 Select (C) helps marginally but CSV is still row-oriented and unpartitioned. Result caching (D) only helps for repeated identical queries and doesn't reduce the cost of initial scans.

stem: A company is migrating a workload from Azure to AWS. The workload uses Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL data storage, Azure Functions for serverless compute, Azure Blob Storage for object storage, and Azure Application Gateway for load balancing. Which set of AWS services provides equivalent functionality for this migration?

options.text: Use Amazon Neptune for Cosmos DB graph data migration, Step Functions for serverless orchestration, S3 Glacier for blob storage, and CloudFront for global traffic distribution and caching.
Use Amazon DocumentDB for Cosmos DB migration, Lambda for serverless compute, S3 for blob storage, and Network Load Balancer for high-performance layer-4 load balancing of API traffic.
Use DynamoDB for NoSQL storage, Lambda for serverless compute, S3 for object storage, and Application Load Balancer for HTTP load balancing with path-based routing and health checks.
Use Amazon Keyspaces for Cosmos DB Cassandra API data, ECS Fargate for serverless containers instead of functions, EFS for file storage, and API Gateway for request routing to services.

explanation: DynamoDB is the closest equivalent to Cosmos DB for general NoSQL workloads with global distribution capability. Lambda maps directly to Azure Functions. S3 maps to Azure Blob Storage. ALB provides the same L7 load balancing as Azure Application Gateway. DocumentDB (B) only covers the MongoDB API of Cosmos DB and NLB doesn't provide L7 features. Keyspaces (C) only covers Cassandra API and ECS Fargate is containers, not functions. Neptune (D) is only for graph data and Glacier is archival, not general blob storage.

stem: A company needs to implement network segmentation across its AWS environment to comply with PCI DSS requirements. The cardholder data environment (CDE) must be isolated from other network segments. Only specific services in the CDE segment can communicate with the payment processor, and all traffic in and out of the CDE must be logged and inspected. Which network architecture provides PCI-compliant segmentation?

options.text: Deploy the CDE in a separate AWS account with its own VPC, connect to the main environment via Transit Gateway with CDE-specific route tables, and log all transit traffic for auditing.
Deploy all resources in a single VPC with separate subnets for CDE and non-CDE, use NACLs to restrict traffic between subnets, and configure VPC Flow Logs for compliance reporting.
Deploy CDE resources in a public subnet with strict security groups allowing only payment processor IPs, enable VPC Flow Logs for auditing, and use WAF for application-layer inspection.
Deploy the CDE in a dedicated VPC with no internet gateway, use AWS PrivateLink for payment processor connectivity, deploy Network Firewall for traffic inspection, and enable VPC Flow Logs.

explanation: A dedicated VPC with no internet gateway provides strong isolation. PrivateLink enables private connectivity to the payment processor without internet exposure. Network Firewall inspects all CDE traffic. VPC Flow Logs provide the audit trail. Public subnet (B) violates PCI DSS by exposing the CDE to the internet. Single VPC with NACLs (C) doesn't provide sufficient isolation for PCI compliance. Separate account with Transit Gateway (D) provides account-level isolation but Transit Gateway adds potential traffic paths that need inspection.

stem: A company is building a data warehouse that must support both structured SQL queries from BI tools and unstructured data analysis from data scientists. The warehouse must integrate with Jupyter notebooks, support machine learning training on warehouse data, and provide governed data sharing with external partners. Which architecture provides all these capabilities in a unified platform?

options.text: Use Amazon EMR with Spark SQL for both structured and unstructured queries, Spark MLlib for machine learning, and create S3 pre-signed URLs for data sharing with external partners.
Use Amazon Redshift with Redshift ML for in-database machine learning, Redshift data sharing for external partners, and integration with SageMaker notebooks and BI tools via JDBC/ODBC connections.
Use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL for structured queries, export data to S3 for ML training with SageMaker, and create a custom API for partner data sharing using API Gateway and Lambda.
Use Amazon Athena for SQL queries on S3 data, SageMaker for ML training, Lake Formation for data sharing with partners, and connect BI tools to Athena via JDBC for structured reporting.

explanation: Redshift provides a unified data warehouse with SQL support for BI tools, Redshift ML for in-database machine learning, native data sharing for governed external partner access, and SageMaker notebook integration. All capabilities in one platform. Athena with SageMaker (B) requires separate services for each capability without the unified warehouse experience. Aurora (C) is OLTP, not a data warehouse, and lacks native data sharing. EMR with Spark (D) requires managing infrastructure and pre-signed URLs don't provide governed data sharing.

stem: A company operates a serverless application using API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB. The application experiences periodic throttling errors from DynamoDB during flash sales. The DynamoDB table uses provisioned capacity with auto-scaling, but auto-scaling reacts too slowly for the sudden traffic spikes. The company wants to handle flash sale traffic without over-provisioning during normal periods. Which capacity strategy best handles this pattern?

options.text: Increase the auto-scaling target utilization from 70% to 90% to keep more headroom for spikes, decrease the scale-up cooldown period to 1 minute, and increase the maximum provisioned capacity.
Keep provisioned capacity with auto-scaling, but schedule capacity increases before known flash sales using Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions to pre-warm the table for expected traffic.
Switch the DynamoDB table to on-demand capacity mode which handles traffic spikes instantly without pre-provisioning, accepting the higher per-request cost during normal traffic periods.
Add a DAX cluster in front of DynamoDB to absorb read traffic during spikes, keeping provisioned capacity for writes only, and configure DAX with a shorter TTL for frequently changing data.

explanation: Scheduled scaling pre-warms DynamoDB capacity before known flash sale events, handling the spike without auto-scaling delay. Normal periods use standard auto-scaling at lower provisioned levels. This optimizes cost while ensuring capacity for known events. On-demand (A) handles spikes but costs more during the majority of normal traffic. Higher target utilization (C) still can't react fast enough for flash spikes. DAX (D) helps reads but doesn't address write throttling during flash sales.

stem: A company runs a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) application that requires a Windows Server environment with Active Directory, SQL Server, and .NET Framework. The application vendor does not support containerization or cloud-native databases. The company wants to migrate to AWS with the lowest possible operational overhead while maintaining vendor support. Which migration approach meets these constraints?

options.text: Containerize the application on ECS with Windows containers, deploy SQL Server on RDS, configure AWS Directory Service for AD, and use Application Load Balancer for HTTP routing.
Deploy the application on EC2 Windows instances joined to AWS Managed Microsoft AD, use RDS for SQL Server for the database, and configure ALB for load balancing with ACM certificates.
Deploy the application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk Windows platform, use Aurora PostgreSQL as the database with a SQL Server compatibility layer, and use Beanstalk's built-in load balancing.
Deploy the application on EC2 Windows instances with self-managed Active Directory on EC2, install SQL Server locally on the application EC2 instances, and configure a Network Load Balancer.

explanation: EC2 Windows instances with Managed Microsoft AD provide the required Windows/AD environment. RDS for SQL Server reduces database operational overhead as a managed service. ALB provides load balancing. This maintains vendor support while minimizing operations. Self-managed AD on EC2 (B) increases operational overhead. Containerization (C) is explicitly not supported by the vendor. Aurora PostgreSQL (D) is not SQL Server and would break vendor support requirements.

stem: A company wants to implement automated incident response for common security events. When GuardDuty detects an EC2 instance communicating with a known command-and-control server, the response must automatically isolate the instance from the network, create a forensic snapshot of the instance's volumes, and notify the security team. Which automation architecture implements this response?

options.text: Configure GuardDuty to export findings to S3, trigger an Athena query every 5 minutes to check for new C2 findings, and invoke a Lambda function for remediation when findings are detected.
Use AWS Config rules to detect GuardDuty findings, configure auto-remediation with SSM Automation documents that isolate instances and create snapshots, and send SNS alerts on completion.
Configure GuardDuty to send findings to EventBridge, trigger a Step Functions workflow that isolates the instance by replacing security groups, snapshots EBS volumes, and sends SNS notifications.
Configure GuardDuty to send findings to CloudWatch Logs, create a metric filter for C2 findings, trigger a CloudWatch alarm that invokes a Lambda function for isolation and notification.

explanation: EventBridge natively receives GuardDuty findings in real-time. Step Functions orchestrates the multi-step response: security group replacement for isolation, EBS snapshot for forensics, and SNS for notification. This provides reliable, ordered execution of all response steps. CloudWatch Logs with metric filters (B) adds unnecessary latency and complexity. Config rules (C) don't directly receive GuardDuty findings. Athena polling every 5 minutes (D) is too slow for security incident response.

stem: A company needs to deploy an application that requires persistent block storage with the ability to take application-consistent snapshots without stopping the application. The storage must deliver 64,000 IOPS with 1,000 MB/s throughput and 99.999% durability. The application runs on a Nitro-based EC2 instance. Which storage configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Use instance store NVMe volumes for maximum IOPS performance, implement application-level replication to S3 for durability, and use custom scripts to create consistent backup points to S3.
Use Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with SSD storage tier, configure iSCSI LUNs for block-level access, use ONTAP Snapshot for application-consistent snapshots, and mount on the EC2 instance.
Use Amazon EBS gp3 volumes with baseline IOPS of 3,000, provision additional IOPS up to 16,000, and create regular EBS snapshots during low-traffic maintenance windows for consistency.
Use Amazon EBS io2 Block Express volumes with 64,000 provisioned IOPS and 1,000 MB/s throughput, create application-consistent snapshots using VSS-enabled EBS snapshot with SSM integration.

explanation: EBS io2 Block Express supports up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MB/s throughput on Nitro instances, meeting the 64K IOPS requirement. It provides 99.999% durability. VSS-enabled snapshots via SSM create application-consistent snapshots without stopping the application. gp3 volumes (B) max out at 16,000 IOPS, insufficient. Instance store (C) provides no durability—data is lost on stop. FSx for ONTAP (D) adds network latency for block storage access compared to directly attached EBS.

stem: A company's EKS cluster runs 200 pods across 20 nodes. The cluster has uneven resource utilization—some nodes are at 90% CPU while others are at 20%. Pod scheduling places new pods on nodes with available resources, but doesn't rebalance existing pods. This causes hot spots and occasional OOM kills on overloaded nodes. Which approach improves resource distribution across the cluster?

options.text: Increase the number of nodes in the cluster from 20 to 40 to reduce overall utilization, even if some nodes remain underutilized, and keep the existing pod scheduling configuration unchanged.
Configure resource requests and limits on all pods to equal their peak usage, preventing any pod from being scheduled on a node without sufficient peak resources reserved for every container.

Deploy the Kubernetes Descheduler to periodically evict pods from overloaded nodes, allowing the scheduler to redistribute them, and configure pod disruption budgets to ensure availability during rebalancing.
Replace EKS managed node groups with Fargate profiles for all pods, eliminating the need for node-level resource management by running each pod in its own isolated compute environment.

explanation: The Descheduler identifies and evicts pods from overloaded or underutilized nodes, allowing the Kubernetes scheduler to redistribute them more evenly. Pod disruption budgets ensure service availability during rebalancing. Doubling nodes (B) wastes resources without addressing the distribution problem. Setting requests equal to peak (C) wastes resources since most pods don't use peak constantly. Fargate for all pods (D) significantly increases cost and doesn't support all workload types.

stem: A company wants to migrate its Jenkins-based CI/CD pipeline to AWS-native services. The pipeline builds Java applications, runs unit and integration tests, creates Docker images, pushes to a registry, and deploys to Kubernetes clusters. The pipeline uses Jenkins shared libraries for common build logic and Jenkinsfiles for pipeline definitions. Which AWS-native replacement provides equivalent CI/CD functionality?

options.text: Use GitHub Actions for CI/CD pipeline definition, CodeBuild for Java builds, ECR for Docker images, and Flux on EKS for continuous deployment, with GitHub reusable workflows for shared logic.
Deploy Jenkins on ECS Fargate with auto-scaling build agents, keep existing Jenkinsfiles and shared libraries, store images in ECR, and configure Jenkins Kubernetes plugin for EKS deployments.
Use CodePipeline for orchestration, CodeBuild for all build stages, ECR for images, and ArgoCD on EKS for GitOps-based Kubernetes deployments, with CDK Pipelines for pipeline-as-code definitions.
Use CodePipeline for orchestration, CodeBuild with buildspec.yml for builds and tests, ECR for Docker images, and CodeDeploy for EKS deployments, with CodeBuild shared projects for common logic.

explanation: CodePipeline replaces Jenkins orchestration. CodeBuild with buildspec.yml replaces Jenkins build stages and shared projects replace shared libraries. ECR replaces the Docker registry. CodeDeploy supports EKS deployment. This is fully AWS-native. ArgoCD/CDK Pipelines (B) adds complexity beyond what's needed for a direct migration. Jenkins on ECS (C) doesn't migrate to AWS-native services. GitHub Actions (D) relies on a non-AWS service for the core CI/CD pipeline.

stem: A company needs to implement a backup strategy that covers all critical resources across 50 AWS accounts. The strategy must include EC2 instances, RDS databases, EFS file systems, and DynamoDB tables. Backups must be encrypted, stored cross-Region for DR, retained for 1 year, and centrally managed. Which solution provides centralized backup management across all accounts?

options.text: Create CloudFormation StackSets that deploy AWS Backup vaults and plans in each account, configure cross-Region vault replication, and use EventBridge to monitor backup completion across accounts.
Use AWS Backup in each account independently, configure identical backup plans manually in each account, enable cross-Region copy in each plan, and aggregate status in a CloudWatch dashboard.
Deploy AWS Backup with a backup policy defined in AWS Organizations, enable cross-account management, configure backup plans with cross-Region copy rules, and set retention to 365 days.
Build a custom backup solution using Lambda functions triggered by EventBridge schedules, create EBS snapshots and RDS snapshots in each account, and copy to a central DR Region account.

explanation: AWS Backup with Organizations integration provides centralized backup policy management from the management account. Policies automatically apply across all accounts. Cross-account management enables monitoring from one location. Cross-Region copy rules handle DR. StackSets (B) deploy plans but don't provide centralized management and monitoring. Custom Lambda solution (C) requires building and maintaining backup logic for each service type. Manual per-account backup (D) doesn't scale to 50 accounts and risks configuration drift.

stem: A company is designing a system that processes insurance claims. Each claim goes through intake, validation, assessment, and approval stages. Claims may take 1-30 days to process and require human review at the assessment stage. The system must track the state of each claim, handle timeouts for SLA compliance, and support parallel processing of multiple assessment criteria. Which orchestration service manages this long-running workflow?

options.text: Use SQS queues between each processing stage with Lambda consumers, track claim state in DynamoDB, implement timeout monitoring with EventBridge scheduled rules, and use SNS for notifications.
Use Step Functions Express Workflows for high-throughput claim processing, callback patterns for human review, and CloudWatch alarms for SLA timeout monitoring across all active claims.
Use AWS Step Functions Standard Workflows with wait states for human review, parallel states for assessment criteria, and timeout configurations for SLA tracking on each state in the workflow.
Use Amazon MWAA (Airflow) to define claim processing DAGs, configure Airflow sensors for human review wait states, and use Airflow SLA monitoring for timeout compliance tracking.

explanation: Step Functions Standard Workflows support executions up to 1 year (covering 30 days), wait states for human review with callbacks, parallel states for multiple assessment criteria, and built-in timeout configuration per state for SLA tracking. Express Workflows (B) have a 5-minute maximum duration, far too short for 1-30 day claims. SQS with DynamoDB (C) requires building the orchestration state machine manually. MWAA (D) is designed for data pipeline orchestration, not long-running business process workflows with human interactions.

stem: A company has an ECS cluster with 50 services. Each service uses its own task definition with a unique Docker image from ECR. The team deploys updates to all 50 services weekly. Currently, each service is deployed manually through the ECS console, which takes the entire day and is error-prone. The company wants to automate deployments for all services. Which automation approach handles multi-service deployments efficiently?

options.text: Create a custom deployment Lambda function triggered by ECR push events that updates the ECS service task definition and triggers a rolling update for the corresponding service automatically.
Create a single CodePipeline with 50 parallel deploy stages, each deploying one ECS service using CodeDeploy with blue/green deployment, triggered by ECR image push events for each service.

Write a shell script that iterates through all 50 services, updates each task definition with the new image URI, and calls ecs:UpdateService for each service, executing the script from a bastion host.
Use AWS CDK Pipelines with a single pipeline that defines all 50 services as deployment stages, deploy sequentially with approval gates between critical services, and use CDK for IaC management.

explanation: ECR push event-triggered Lambda automatically detects new images and updates the corresponding ECS service. This provides event-driven, per-service deployment automation without managing 50 separate pipelines. Each service deploys independently when its image is pushed. A single CodePipeline with 50 stages (A) is complex to manage and tightly couples all services. CDK Pipelines sequentially (B) creates unnecessarily long deployment times. Shell scripts from bastion (D) is manual and not automated.

stem: A company runs a legacy application on IBM WebSphere Application Server. The application uses Java EE features including EJBs, JMS, and JNDI. The company wants to migrate to AWS while modernizing the application server platform. The application code should require minimal changes. Which migration target maintains Java EE compatibility?

options.text: Migrate the application to AWS Elastic Beanstalk Tomcat platform, convert EJBs to servlets, replace JMS with Amazon MQ integration, and update JNDI lookups to AWS-specific resource names.
Deploy the application on Amazon ECS using the Open Liberty container image, which supports Java EE and Jakarta EE features, and configure the Liberty server for EJB, JMS, and JNDI support.
Deploy IBM WebSphere Application Server on EC2 instances, maintaining the existing runtime environment, and use BYOL licensing to reduce costs compared to the on-premises deployment.
Rewrite the application to use Spring Boot, replacing EJBs with Spring beans, JMS with SQS SDK calls, and JNDI with Spring dependency injection, then deploy on Lambda with API Gateway.

explanation: Open Liberty is the open-source version of WebSphere Liberty Profile and supports full Java EE/Jakarta EE features including EJBs, JMS, and JNDI. Running on ECS provides managed container orchestration. Minimal code changes are needed. Spring Boot rewrite (B) is a major refactoring effort. WebSphere on EC2 (C) doesn't modernize the platform. Tomcat (D) doesn't support EJBs, requiring significant application changes.

stem: A company needs to enable developers to provision their own development environments on-demand while ensuring all environments conform to security standards. Environments must include a VPC with specific CIDR ranges, pre-configured security groups, an RDS database, and an ECS cluster. Environments should be automatically cleaned up after 30 days. Which self-service mechanism provides governed environment provisioning?

options.text: Provide developers with CloudFormation templates in a shared S3 bucket, document the deployment instructions in a wiki, and remind developers via email to clean up environments after 30 days.

Create AWS Service Catalog products for each environment type with CloudFormation templates, add tag options for tracking, configure a scheduled Lambda function to terminate environments after 30 days.
Deploy AWS Control Tower Account Factory to provision dedicated accounts per developer environment, configure guardrails for security compliance, and close accounts after 30 days automatically.
Create a custom web portal on Amplify that deploys environments using CDK, store environment metadata in DynamoDB, and implement a CloudWatch Events rule to trigger cleanup after 30 days.

explanation: Service Catalog provides a self-service portal with pre-approved CloudFormation templates ensuring compliance. Launch constraints control what developers can deploy. Tag options enable tracking. Scheduled Lambda handles automatic cleanup. Shared templates (B) don't enforce standards and rely on developer discipline. Account Factory per environment (C) is expensive and over-engineered for development environments. Custom Amplify portal (D) requires building and maintaining a custom application.

stem: A company is building a data processing pipeline that must guarantee exactly-once processing of records from a Kinesis Data Stream. The pipeline transforms records and writes results to both DynamoDB and S3. If the Lambda consumer fails mid-batch, records must not be duplicated in either destination. Which approach ensures exactly-once semantics end-to-end?

options.text: Use Kinesis Data Firehose for automatic S3 delivery with deduplication, and a separate Lambda consumer for DynamoDB writes with the Kinesis event source configured for at-most-once delivery.

Use Lambda with Kinesis event source mapping, implement idempotent writes to DynamoDB using conditional expressions on a unique record ID, and use S3 object keys based on record IDs for deduplication.
Use Kinesis enhanced fan-out with dedicated throughput per consumer, configure Lambda with bisect-on-failure for error handling, and implement automatic checkpointing for processed records.
Use Amazon MSK instead of Kinesis for exactly-once transactional processing, consume with Kafka Streams that provides built-in exactly-once semantics, and write to both DynamoDB and S3 atomically.

explanation: Idempotent writes with conditional expressions in DynamoDB ensure that reprocessed records don't create duplicates. S3 writes with deterministic keys based on record IDs overwrite rather than duplicate. Together these provide exactly-once semantics despite at-least-once delivery from Kinesis. Enhanced fan-out and bisect (B) improve processing but don't provide exactly-once guarantees. Firehose (C) doesn't coordinate with DynamoDB writes. MSK exactly-once (D) covers Kafka internal processing but not cross-service writes to DynamoDB and S3.

stem: A company uses Amazon Aurora MySQL with ProxySQL on EC2 for read/write splitting. The ProxySQL layer adds operational overhead and occasional failures cause application outages. The company wants to eliminate the ProxySQL management while maintaining read/write splitting capability. Which AWS-managed solution replaces ProxySQL?

options.text: Deploy a second Application Load Balancer with routing rules that direct SELECT queries to reader endpoints and write queries to the writer endpoint based on HTTP request method.
Deploy Amazon RDS Proxy with Aurora MySQL endpoint configuration, enable read/write splitting via proxy endpoints, point the application to the proxy endpoint, and remove ProxySQL instances.
Use Route 53 weighted routing between the Aurora writer and reader endpoints, configure health checks on both endpoints, and let DNS load balancing distribute queries automatically.
Modify the application to use Aurora reader and writer endpoints directly, implement read/write detection in the application connection pool, and remove ProxySQL from the architecture.

explanation: RDS Proxy provides managed read/write splitting as a direct replacement for ProxySQL. The application connects to a single proxy endpoint, and RDS Proxy routes reads to replicas and writes to the writer automatically. No application code changes needed. Application-level splitting (B) requires code changes. ALB for database routing (C) is not architecturally appropriate—ALBs handle HTTP, not database protocol traffic. Route 53 DNS (D) doesn't understand SQL query types for read/write routing.

stem: A company is migrating a real-time analytics dashboard from on-premises to AWS. The dashboard displays key metrics updated every 5 seconds from a PostgreSQL database. The current architecture polls the database every 5 seconds from a React frontend. The migration must reduce database load from dashboard polling while maintaining 5-second refresh rates. Which architecture eliminates database polling?

options.text: Use Aurora PostgreSQL with DynamoDB Streams-style change data capture through Aurora activity streams, process changes with Lambda, and push updates to the React frontend via AppSync subscriptions.
Deploy the React frontend on Amplify with a scheduled Lambda that queries Aurora every 5 seconds, stores results in S3, and serves the static JSON files through CloudFront for the dashboard.
Use Aurora PostgreSQL with logical replication to capture data changes, process change events with Lambda, cache current metrics in ElastiCache, and poll ElastiCache from the frontend instead.
Use Aurora PostgreSQL with AWS DMS CDC to capture changes, write processed metrics to DynamoDB, and use AppSync with DynamoDB resolver and real-time subscriptions to push updates to the frontend.

explanation: DMS CDC captures database changes without polling. DynamoDB stores current metrics efficiently. AppSync subscriptions push real-time updates to the React frontend, eliminating all polling. This is the event-driven approach that reduces database load. Aurora activity streams (A) are for audit logging, not general CDC for application use. Logical replication to Lambda with ElastiCache (B) still requires polling from the frontend. Scheduled Lambda querying Aurora (D) still polls the database every 5 seconds.

stem: A company runs sensitive workloads that require all compute instances to be launched only from approved AMIs. The approved AMIs are maintained by the security team in a shared services account. The security team needs to distribute AMIs to all accounts, ensure only approved AMIs can be used for instance launches, and automatically deprecate old AMI versions. Which approach enforces approved AMI usage?

options.text: Copy approved AMIs to each account using Lambda automation, create IAM policies per account allowing only specific AMI IDs for RunInstances, and delete old copies when AMIs are deprecated.
Share approved AMIs via AWS RAM from the shared services account, create an SCP that restricts ec2:RunInstances to only the shared AMI IDs using the ec2:ImageId condition key.
Store approved AMI IDs in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, reference parameters in CloudFormation templates, and require all instance launches to use CloudFormation with approved templates.
Publish approved AMIs to AWS Marketplace as private products, require all accounts to launch instances only from the Marketplace listing, and delist deprecated versions from the Marketplace.

explanation: RAM sharing distributes AMIs centrally without copying to each account. SCPs with ec2:ImageId condition prevent launching instances from unapproved AMIs across all accounts. Deprecating AMIs in the source account updates access everywhere. Copying AMIs per account (B) creates management overhead for 50+ accounts and IAM policies can be modified by admins. Marketplace (C) adds unnecessary complexity for internal AMI distribution. Parameter Store with CloudFormation (D) doesn't prevent direct instance launches outside CloudFormation.

stem: A company is designing a system to detect anomalies in financial transaction patterns in near real-time. The system must process 50,000 transactions per second, apply ML models for anomaly scoring, correlate transactions across accounts to detect ring fraud patterns, and alert investigators within 30 seconds of detection. Which architecture processes transactions at this speed with ML inference?

options.text: Ingest transactions to S3 via Kinesis Data Firehose in micro-batches, run SageMaker batch transform for ML scoring every minute, query results with Athena, and send alerts via SNS.
Use Kinesis Data Streams for ingestion, Kinesis Data Analytics with Apache Flink for windowed analysis and ML inference using pre-trained models, and SNS for investigator alerting.
Use Amazon MSK for transaction ingestion, deploy ML models on Kafka Streams consumer applications running on ECS, store correlation state in Redis, and alert via Amazon Connect.
Use SQS for transaction queuing, Lambda for ML inference calling SageMaker endpoints, DynamoDB for cross-account correlation, and EventBridge for routing alerts to the investigation team.

explanation: Kinesis Data Streams handles 50K TPS with shard scaling. Kinesis Data Analytics with Flink provides stateful stream processing with windowed analysis for pattern correlation and integrated ML inference. Sub-30-second latency is achievable. SNS delivers alerts. SQS with Lambda (B) can't maintain state for cross-account correlation across transactions. Firehose micro-batches with batch transform (C) adds too much latency for 30-second alerting. MSK with Kafka Streams (D) works but requires more operational management than the managed Kinesis/Flink approach.

stem: A company's production EKS cluster has 50 namespaces, each belonging to a different team. Teams frequently create deployments that consume excessive resources, affecting other teams' workloads. There are no resource controls in place. The company needs to implement resource isolation between teams while still sharing the cluster infrastructure. Which Kubernetes and AWS controls provide multi-tenant resource isolation?

options.text: Deploy AWS Fargate profiles per namespace, eliminating node sharing entirely by running each pod in its own Fargate task, and use IAM roles for service accounts for access isolation.
Implement ResourceQuotas per namespace to limit CPU, memory, and pod count per team, configure LimitRanges for default resource requests, and use network policies for namespace traffic isolation.
Migrate from a single shared EKS cluster to 50 separate EKS clusters (one per team) to provide complete isolation, manage clusters centrally using EKS Anywhere for unified management.
Create separate node groups per team using EKS managed node groups with taints and tolerations, dedicate specific EC2 instance types to each team, and use RBAC for access control.

explanation: ResourceQuotas enforce per-namespace CPU, memory, and pod limits preventing any team from consuming excessive resources. LimitRanges set defaults for pods without explicit requests. Network policies isolate inter-namespace traffic. These are the standard Kubernetes multi-tenancy controls. Separate node groups (B) waste resources since nodes can't be shared. 50 separate clusters (C) is extremely expensive and operationally complex. Fargate profiles (D) significantly increase costs and don't support all workload types.

stem: A company is migrating a large-scale web application that currently handles sessions, caching, and real-time features using a self-managed Redis cluster on-premises. The Redis cluster has 12 nodes in a cluster mode configuration with 6 shards and replication. The company wants a managed replacement that maintains Redis cluster mode compatibility. Which AWS service provides a direct replacement?

options.text: Deploy Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in cluster mode with 6 shards and 1 replica per shard, configure node types matching the on-premises capacity, and migrate data using redis-cli migration.
Deploy Amazon DynamoDB with DAX for caching to replace Redis functionality, redesign the caching strategy around DynamoDB's key-value model, and use DynamoDB Streams for real-time features.
Deploy Amazon MemoryDB for Redis in cluster mode for durable data storage, configure 6 shards with replicas, and use the Redis-compatible API for seamless application migration.
Deploy Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with 12 nodes for caching, use DynamoDB for session storage, and replace Redis pub/sub with Amazon SNS for real-time messaging features.

explanation: ElastiCache for Redis in cluster mode directly replaces the on-premises Redis cluster with identical shard/replica topology and full Redis API compatibility. redis-cli enables data migration. No application changes needed. MemoryDB (B) provides durability but is designed for primary database use and is more expensive for caching workloads. DynamoDB with DAX (C) requires redesigning the entire caching strategy. Memcached (D) doesn't support Redis features like sorted sets, pub/sub, and cluster mode.

stem: A company needs to implement an automated compliance check that runs before any CloudFormation stack is created or updated in production accounts. The check must validate that the template complies with company security policies (no public S3 buckets, encryption enabled on all storage, no wildcard IAM policies). Non-compliant stacks must be blocked from deployment. Which mechanism provides pre-deployment compliance validation?

options.text: Use CloudFormation Guard in the CI/CD pipeline to validate templates before deployment, blocking the pipeline on policy violations, and require all deployments to go through the pipeline.
Deploy AWS Config rules that detect non-compliant resources after creation, configure auto-remediation to fix violations, and accept a brief window where non-compliant resources may exist.
Register CloudFormation hooks that invoke a Lambda function to validate templates against security policies before resource provisioning, failing the stack operation if any violation is detected.
Implement SCPs that deny creating non-compliant resources using condition keys for encryption and public access, covering all resource creation regardless of whether CloudFormation is used.

explanation: CloudFormation hooks intercept stack operations and validate templates before any resources are provisioned. Non-compliant stacks are blocked at the CloudFormation level, working even for console deployments. Config rules (B) are reactive, allowing non-compliant resources to exist temporarily. Guard in CI/CD (C) only catches violations in pipeline deployments, not console or CLI-based CloudFormation operations. SCPs (D) can enforce some policies but cannot validate complex template properties like IAM policy content.

stem: A company is building an e-commerce platform that requires PCI DSS compliance for payment processing. The platform must encrypt all cardholder data, restrict network access to the payment processing components, and maintain detailed audit logs of all access to cardholder data. Which TWO architectural decisions are essential for PCI DSS compliance?

options.text: Encrypt cardholder data using AWS KMS customer managed keys with automatic rotation, enable CloudTrail data events on all S3 buckets and DynamoDB tables storing cardholder data.
Deploy all e-commerce components including product catalog and user profiles in the same isolated VPC as payment processing to simplify network architecture and reduce management overhead.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights for monitoring ECS containers running payment services, configure custom dashboards for transaction volume, and set up SNS alerts for anomalies.
Deploy payment processing components in an isolated VPC segment with no internet gateway, use VPC endpoints for AWS service access, and implement Network Firewall for traffic inspection.

explanation: Network isolation of payment components with no internet access and firewall inspection meets PCI DSS network segmentation requirements. KMS encryption with rotation and CloudTrail data events provide the encryption and audit logging requirements. Container monitoring (C) provides operational visibility but doesn't address PCI-specific requirements. Deploying all components together (D) violates PCI's principle of minimizing the cardholder data environment scope.

stem: A company uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a data processing pipeline. The pipeline has grown to 100 states and exceeds the 256 KB state machine definition limit. The team cannot simplify the workflow as each state represents a necessary processing step. Which approach allows the pipeline to continue growing beyond the definition size limit?

options.text: Replace Step Functions with SQS queues between each processing step, implement state tracking in DynamoDB, and use Lambda functions to manage the workflow progression through all 100 states.
Decompose the single state machine into multiple child state machines, use the Step Functions StartExecution action to call child state machines from a parent orchestrator, passing data between them.
Reduce the state machine definition size by compressing state names, removing comments, and minimizing the JSON structure, and continue adding states within the optimized definition limit.
Migrate from Step Functions to Amazon MWAA (Airflow) which has no practical DAG size limit, convert the state machine definition to an Airflow DAG, and deploy on a managed Airflow environment.

explanation: Nested state machines allow decomposition into logical sub-workflows, each within the size limit. The parent state machine orchestrates child executions, passing data between them. This is the Step Functions pattern for large workflows. Airflow migration (B) requires converting the entire workflow and managing a new service. JSON minimization (C) provides minimal savings and isn't scalable. SQS-based state management (D) requires building a custom orchestration engine, losing Step Functions' built-in error handling and visualization.

stem: A company is migrating a complex enterprise resource planning (ERP) system that integrates with 20 internal and external systems through file-based integrations (SFTP), API calls (REST/SOAP), and database links. The company wants to decouple these integrations during migration to prevent a big-bang cutover of all connected systems. Which integration pattern enables gradual system-by-system migration?

options.text: Deploy MuleSoft Anypoint Platform on EC2 as an enterprise integration bus, route all system connections through MuleSoft, and migrate backend systems from on-premises to AWS one at a time.
Deploy AWS Transfer Family for file-based integrations, API Gateway for REST/SOAP APIs, and DMS for database links, creating an integration layer that abstracts the ERP from connected systems.
Deploy Amazon EventBridge as a central event bus, create event-driven integrations for each system, migrate systems one at a time from direct connections to event-based communication patterns.
Use AWS AppFlow for SaaS integrations, configure bi-directional data flows between the ERP and connected systems, and migrate flows one at a time from direct connections to AppFlow-managed flows.

explanation: Transfer Family handles SFTP integrations, API Gateway provides REST/SOAP facades, and DMS manages database links—covering all three integration patterns. This abstraction layer allows each connected system to be migrated independently without changing others. EventBridge (A) is for event-driven architectures but doesn't handle file-based or database link integrations natively. AppFlow (C) is limited to specific SaaS connectors, not general SFTP/SOAP/database integrations. MuleSoft on EC2 (D) requires managing additional infrastructure.

stem: A company with strict data classification policies needs to prevent any classified data from being stored in unapproved AWS Regions. The company uses Amazon Macie to classify S3 data, but needs a mechanism to automatically move misplaced classified data to the approved Region and delete the non-compliant copy. Which approach automates data residency enforcement?

options.text: Use S3 Replication rules to automatically copy all data to the approved Region, then run scheduled Lambda functions to delete data in unapproved Regions after confirming replication completion.
Configure Macie to detect classified data in unapproved Regions, trigger EventBridge rules on findings that invoke Step Functions to copy the data to the approved Region and delete the original copy.
Deploy AWS Config rules to detect S3 objects in unapproved Regions, generate compliance reports for the security team, and require manual remediation within 48 hours per company policy.
Implement SCPs that completely deny all S3 actions in unapproved Regions, preventing any data from being stored outside approved Regions regardless of classification level in the first place.

explanation: Macie identifies classified data specifically, EventBridge triggers on classification findings, and Step Functions orchestrates the copy-then-delete remediation workflow automatically. This targets only classified data, not all data. S3 Replication (B) copies all data regardless of classification. SCPs (C) block all S3 operations which may be needed for non-classified data in other Regions. Config rules with manual remediation (D) don't automate the move and have a 48-hour delay.

stem: A company is designing a platform for deploying machine learning models that supports A/B testing between model versions. The platform must route a configurable percentage of inference requests to each model version, collect performance metrics per version, and automatically promote the better-performing version. Which architecture supports ML model A/B testing?

options.text: Deploy each model version as a separate Lambda function behind API Gateway, use API Gateway canary deployments to split traffic, and manually compare CloudWatch metrics to determine the winner.
Deploy models on separate ECS services behind an ALB, configure target group weights for traffic splitting, monitor with CloudWatch custom metrics, and use CodeDeploy for promotion.
Deploy models on SageMaker endpoints with production variants, configure traffic splitting between model versions, use CloudWatch metrics per variant, and implement auto-promotion with Lambda.
Deploy both model versions on a single EC2 instance, implement traffic splitting in application code using random number generation, log metrics to CloudWatch, and redeploy the better version.

explanation: SageMaker production variants natively support traffic splitting between model versions on the same endpoint. CloudWatch provides per-variant metrics (latency, error rate, invocation count). Lambda can compare metrics and update variant weights for automatic promotion. API Gateway canary (B) is designed for API code, not ML model versioning. ALB with ECS (C) requires managing infrastructure for each model version. Application-level splitting on EC2 (D) doesn't scale and lacks native model management.

stem: A company runs Amazon MSK for event streaming. The operations team spends significant time managing broker storage scaling, partition rebalancing, and cluster upgrades. During a recent version upgrade, the cluster experienced 30 minutes of partial unavailability. The company wants to reduce MSK operational overhead while maintaining Kafka API compatibility. Which improvement reduces management burden?

options.text: Migrate from MSK to Amazon SQS for all event streaming workloads, replace topic-based consumption with queue-based processing, and eliminate the need for broker management entirely.
Replace MSK with Amazon Kinesis Data Streams which provides serverless streaming without infrastructure management, rewrite producers and consumers to use the Kinesis SDK instead of Kafka clients.

Implement automated MSK management using Lambda functions triggered by CloudWatch alarms for storage scaling, use MSK Connect for partition rebalancing, and schedule upgrades during maintenance windows.
Migrate from MSK provisioned to MSK Serverless which automatically manages broker provisioning, storage scaling, and partition management while maintaining full Kafka API compatibility.

explanation: MSK Serverless eliminates broker management, automatic storage scaling, and partition management while maintaining complete Kafka API compatibility. No producer or consumer code changes needed. Kinesis (B) requires rewriting all Kafka clients to Kinesis SDK. Lambda-based automation (C) adds complexity rather than reducing it. SQS (D) is a different messaging paradigm that doesn't support Kafka features like topic consumption and consumer groups.

stem: A company is migrating a monolithic application that serves both a web frontend and a REST API from the same codebase. The frontend serves HTML pages and the API serves JSON. During migration, the company wants to separate the frontend from the backend API to enable independent scaling and development. Which approach cleanly separates the frontend while maintaining backward compatibility?

options.text: Keep the monolith as-is on EC2, deploy a new React frontend on Amplify that calls the existing monolith API endpoints, and gradually migrate users from the server-rendered HTML to the React SPA.
Extract the HTML frontend to a static React SPA hosted on S3 with CloudFront, deploy the API on ECS Fargate behind API Gateway, and use CloudFront behaviors to route API calls to the backend.
Deploy the monolith on Lambda behind API Gateway, configure Lambda@Edge to serve the HTML frontend from edge locations, and route API calls to the Lambda backend through the same API Gateway.
Deploy the same monolith on two separate ECS service instances, route HTML requests to one set and API requests to the other using ALB path-based routing, scaling each independently.
